mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Tagaloa ‌place ​creator, ocean ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Tagaloa appears ‌in ​polynesian ‌tradition as ​creator, ​ocean. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"The ‌lord", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Tagaloa ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Tagaloa survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Tagaloa ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Tagaloa, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​creator ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Tagaloa** ​(*tagaloa*) — ‌Creator, ‌Ocean · ​The ​lord — ​belongs to ​the ​Polynesian tradition, ‌where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Creator, Ocean". ​The ‌name means ​"The lord"[^1].

​**Tagaloa** ​is the ​supreme ​creator god ‌of ​the Samoan ‌islands, ​lord of ‌the ​layered heavens ‌who looked ​down ‌on the ​empty ​sea and ‌made ‌the land. ‌He ​is **the ​maker ‌of islands, ​the father ​of ‌gods and ​chiefs, ​and the ‌dweller ​in the ‌highest ​sky** — ​the ​figure around ​whom Samoan ‌cosmology ‌turns.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records ‌the canonical ​scholarly ​spelling **Tagaloa** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/tagaloa/). The ‌displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ​computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*tagaloa* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​modern Polynesian ​orthographies; ​macron ​usage follows ​each ‌tradition’s reference ​dictionaries. ​Etymologically ‌the name ​means ‌"The ​lord"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling **Tagaloa** ​matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*tagaloa* contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ‌claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ‌and provenance, ​and ‌keep ​the original ​evidence ​visible. meditation.body: What ​Tagaloa teaches ‌is that ‌creation can ​be ​an act ​of **looking ​down**. His ​world ‌begins not ​with a ​battle or ‌a ​body but ‌with a ​lord in ‌the ​highest heaven ​and an ​empty sea ​— ​and then ‌a decision: ​to let ‌something ​down. Polynesian ‌cosmology is ​famously oceanic, ‌yet ​its supreme ‌god is ​a sky-dweller; ​the ‌islands are ‌the rope ‌and bridge ​between ​the two. ‌This is ​a theology ​suited ‌to navigators: ​the world ​is made ‌of ​layers — ‌sky, sea, ​land, underworld ​— ​and authority ​flows along ‌the vertical ‌axis, ​from above ‌downward, from ​the god ​to ‌the chief ‌to the ‌people. Tagaloa ‌is ​therefore less ‌a 'god ​of' any ​one ​thing than ‌the source ​of rank ​itself: ​where he ‌acts, land ​appears; where ​his ​daughter descends, ‌chiefs are ​born. To ‌study ​him is ‌to see ​how a ‌non-literate ‌society stored ​its constitution ​in cosmology, ​safe ​from conquest, ‌until ethnographers ‌wrote it ​down.[^1]
